ideas.title: Stars don't twinkle. Our air does it.
ideas.angle: Myth-bust the flicker: the star is steady, moving pockets of air bend its single thin ray of light, while a planet's tiny disk sends a bundle of rays whose wobbles average out.

ideas.title: The metal isn't colder. Your hand is.
ideas.angle: Myth-bust the cold spoon: metal and wood in the same room are the same temperature, but metal conducts heat out of your skin far faster, and skin senses its own heat loss rather than the object's temperature.

ideas.title: Why light walks straight through a solid wall of glass
ideas.angle: Visible photons carry 1.6 to 3.1 eV but the electrons in glass need about three times more to jump, so the light is never absorbed and passes through.

ideas.title: Why a yawn you only hear can make you yawn
ideas.angle: Seeing or hearing a yawn switches on brain areas tied to copying actions, so your own yawn programme starts running before you decide; the exact mechanism is still debated.

ideas.title: The ocean isn't reflecting the sky
ideas.angle: Water absorbs longer red wavelengths more strongly while shorter blue wavelengths penetrate and scatter back toward our eyes; the sky-mirror answer fails because the sea stays blue under gray clouds and underwater.

ideas.title: Your skin can't feel wet. Your brain guesses.
ideas.angle: Skin has no wetness receptor. The brain infers wet by combining a cold signal with a light touch signal, which is why a cold dry thing can feel damp and warm water feels less wet than cold water.

ideas.title: The Sun isn't yellow. It's white.
ideas.angle: Sunlight contains every colour, which together look white; our air scatters some blue light away, so from the ground the Sun looks slightly yellow - and that scattered blue is the sky.

ideas.title: Octopus blood isn't red. It's copper blue.
ideas.angle: Octopus blood carries oxygen with copper-based hemocyanin instead of iron-based hemoglobin, so it turns blue while it holds oxygen - and goes clear when it lets go.

ideas.title: The straw isn't broken. The light is bending.
ideas.angle: Light bends when it leaves the water and enters air, and your eye traces it back along a straight line to the wrong place, so the underwater half of the straw seems to sit where it is not.

ideas.title: Helium doesn't change your vocal cords
ideas.angle: Sound travels nearly three times faster in helium, which slides the resonances of your throat and mouth upward, while your vocal cords keep vibrating at about the same pitch.

ideas.title: Your hum dies because the pressure evens out
ideas.angle: Try-it-now explainer: pinch your nose and hum, the sound dies in a second. The vocal folds need air flowing up through them; seal every exit and the pressure above them climbs to match the lungs, so the flow and the buzz stop.

ideas.title: Every goose surfs the bird in front
ideas.angle: Explainer: each wingtip spins off a swirl; behind and to the side the air rises. The V puts every follower in that rising air, and GPS-tracked ibises even timed their flaps to the bird ahead.

ideas.title: A hotter pan keeps water alive longer
ideas.angle: Myth-bust 'hotter always evaporates faster': above about 200 °C a drop floats on its own steam, skates around and lasts far longer than on a merely hot pan.

ideas.title: That plug isn't looking at you
ideas.angle: Your brain runs a crude, fast face detector (two eyes above a mouth) that fires on plugs and clouds; it's tuned to false alarms because missing a real face costs more.

ideas.title: Cats have a mirror in each eye
ideas.angle: Explainer: the glow is reflected light from the tapetum lucidum behind the retina; it sends light back for a second pass, boosting night vision at the cost of some sharpness; humans don't have it.

ideas.title: That crack is the ice fighting itself
ideas.angle: Explainer: the cube's outer layer warms and expands in the drink while the frozen core does not; the mismatch builds stress, and brittle ice snaps instead of bending.

ideas.title: Your toast isn't cursed. Your table is too short.
ideas.angle: Myth-bust: it's not the butter's weight. Toast tips over the table edge and starts spinning; from table height it only has time for about half a turn, so butter-up becomes butter-down. A table about 3 m tall would flip it right back.

ideas.title: Your skull adds bass only you can hear
ideas.angle: Explainer: you hear yourself through air and through your skull; the skull path boosts low tones; a mic only gets the air path, so the recording sounds thinner and strange to you, but it is close to what others hear.

ideas.title: Your knuckle crack is a bubble, not your bones
ideas.angle: Bust the 'bones grinding' myth: an MRI showed a gas cavity forming; scientists still argue about collapse; and no, it does not cause arthritis.

ideas.title: The man who cracked one hand for 60 years
ideas.angle: Story of a 60-year one-handed experiment.

ideas.title: Why you can't crack the same knuckle twice
ideas.angle: Explain the bubble that stays behind.

ideas.title: Brain freeze isn't your brain freezing
ideas.angle: Explain the mechanism: cold hits the palate, the pain is referred to the forehead, and a small study saw an artery widen as the pain began and narrow as it faded.

ideas.title: Gulp vs sip: the brain freeze experiment
ideas.angle: Compare the two experiments: ice water gulped triggers brain freeze in half of people, an ice cube only in one in eight; fast ice cream doubles it in a school trial.

ideas.title: Why does cold in your mouth hurt your forehead?
ideas.angle: Pose the referred-pain puzzle, answer it, and connect it to migraine-prone people who get brain freeze more often.

ideas.title: Leap years aren't every four years
ideas.angle: Myth-bust the rule everyone learned: the year is 365.2422 days, every-4 leap days overshoot, the drift reached 10 days, and since 1582 century years only leap if they divide by 400.

ideas.title: The ten days that vanished in October 1582
ideas.angle: Tell the calendar's correction as a story: the Julian surplus piled up, Thursday 4 October was followed by Friday 15 October, and Britain skipped 11 days in 1752.

ideas.title: The three leap-year rules in one go
ideas.angle: A fast listicle: divide by 4 to leap, skip century years, but leap again if the year divides by 400, and why the third rule exists.

ideas.title: Was 2000 a leap year?
ideas.angle: A quiz built on the year most people get wrong, answered with the divide-by-400 rule.

ideas.title: A dead flamingo can still stand on one leg
ideas.angle: Myth-bust the 'hard balancing act': in the 2017 cadaver test the one-legged pose held with zero muscle, two legs did not, and live birds swayed less when they dozed.

ideas.title: Two reasons flamingos tuck a leg: warmth and effort
ideas.angle: Explain both supported explanations: more birds rest on one leg in water and in the cold (heat saving), and the pose costs almost no muscle (effort saving).

ideas.title: That backwards knee is an ankle
ideas.angle: Start from the anatomy most people get wrong (the visible joint is the ankle, the knee is hidden) and use it to show how the leg locks into a passive pillar.

ideas.title: One leg or two: which is harder for a flamingo?
ideas.angle: Run the comparison the lab ran: held upright, the body locked on one leg but could not be held stable on two, the opposite of what people expect.

ideas.title: The giant horizon Moon is not bigger
ideas.angle: Myth-bust what everyone has seen: same-settings photos show the same width, the low Moon is even about 1.5 percent farther away, and the size is added by the brain.

ideas.title: Shrink the giant Moon with a paper tube
ideas.angle: A tonight-you-can-try-it video: hold up a fingernail, then look through a paper tube, and watch the illusion collapse.

ideas.title: Why your brain inflates the horizon Moon
ideas.angle: Explain the leading idea: the brain treats the horizon Moon as farther away, so it scales it up; tested since Kaufman and Rock, still debated.

ideas.title: Camera versus eyes: who is right about the Moon?
ideas.angle: Put the camera and the eye side by side: the photo keeps the Moon the same width, the eye does not.

ideas.angle: Myth-bust: no suction cups, no glue; hundreds of thousands of hairs split into tiny tips, and weak forces between molecules add up to a grip that works upside down on glass.
